idiom_name: syslog(3) or systemd journal sink plus a hand-rolled OpenSSL HMAC hash chain
implementation_notes: C has neither a logging chokepoint nor a cryptographic primitive in libc: syslog(3)/openlog() hands messages to the system logger and sd_journal_send() to the journal, but neither lets you key an integrity chain, so the writer, the chain state and the MAC are assembled by hand - normally over OpenSSL's HMAC() or the EVP_MAC API, with an O_APPEND file the application can only append to. The classic hand-written form is justified precisely because nothing replaces it; the realistic alternatives are to delegate the whole guarantee to a platform feature (journald sealing) or to RFC 5848 signed syslog, and to keep only the record construction in C.
pitfalls: syslog(3) and journald record what you send but do not key anything: integrity is still your job unless the platform seals the journal, so never present a plain syslog line as tamper-evident.
The chain state is shared mutable data: two writer threads or a fork()ed child that inherits the state will both continue the chain and produce divergent histories that no verifier can reconcile.

Never pass user-controlled data as the syslog format string (syslog(prio, user_string) is a format-string bug); use "%s" and treat every field as data, and check errno in the failure path before deciding fail-open or fail-closed.
